introduction: On this second-last Sunday of the liturgical year, the readings look to the end of time. Daniel speaks of a time of distress, when the wise will shine like the stars. In the Gospel, Jesus speaks of the Son of Man coming in the clouds and tells us to learn from the fig tree. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away. Let us live in hope, watching for his coming.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord shows us the path of life. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may keep watch in hope and proclaim the words of Christ that will never pass away. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who live in times of distress, war and persecution: that God may protect and deliver them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who turn many to righteousness, teachers, catechists and parents: that they may shine like the stars. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are afraid of the future: that they may find peace in God's faithful love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may set the Lord always before us and be ready for his coming. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, heaven and earth will pass away, but your words will not pass away. Keep us faithful in hope until your Son comes in glory. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: My words will not pass away
reflection.body:
As the Church's year comes to an end, the readings turn our eyes to the end of all things. This can seem frightening, but its message is hope.

Daniel speaks of "a time of trouble, such as never was," but also of deliverance. "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake." This is one of the clearest promises of resurrection in the Old Testament. And those who have lived faithfully will be glorious: "Those who turn many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever."

In the Gospel, Jesus uses the vivid language of the prophets: the sun darkened, the stars falling. But the center of the picture is not destruction. It is Christ: "Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory." He will send his angels to "gather together his chosen ones from the four winds."

Jesus gives us a simple image from nature: when the fig tree puts out leaves, you know summer is near. And he gives us a promise to hold on to: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." Everything else is temporary; his word is not.

He also tells us what we cannot know: "of that day or that hour no one knows." We are not asked to calculate dates but to be ready.

The psalm shows the calm of someone who trusts God: "I have set the LORD always before me. Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."

This week, think about what in your life will pass away and what will last. Spend time with the words of Jesus, which will never pass away. And live each day as if he might come today, not with fear, but with hope.
